name: BNN-20

lead: BNN-20 is a lab-made steroid-like compound, described by its developers as a "microneurotrophin", meant to mimic the brain growth factor BDNF. People in research-chemical circles discuss it for brain protection and cognitive support.

It is derived from DHEA, crosses the blood-brain barrier and is reported to lack endocrine side effects. It acts through the TrkB receptor and reduces neuroinflammation in mouse models, mainly the "weaver" mouse model of Parkinson's-like dopamine neuron loss. No human studies exist and no appearance use is documented.

paras: It is discussed in longevity and nootropic circles as a neurotrophin mimic. There is no established human routine or timeline.
Human safety is unknown because no clinical trials are published. It is not an approved drug.

angle.text: BNN-20 is a DHEA-derived BDNF mimic discussed in research-chemical circles for brain protection and cognitive support. No appearance use is documented; the research is preclinical, mainly Parkinson's mouse models.

lead: BNN-20 is a synthetic compound described by its developers as a "microneurotrophin": a small molecule, 17-beta-spiro-[5-androsten-17,2'-oxiran]-3beta-ol, derived from the hormone DHEA, that crosses the blood-brain barrier and is reported to lack endocrine side effects [1]. It is designed to imitate the protective signalling of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), a protein that large-molecule neurotrophic therapies struggle to deliver into the brain [1][2].

Research has been preclinical, mainly in the "weaver" mouse, a genetic model of progressive dopamine neuron loss in the substantia nigra of the kind seen in Parkinson's disease [1][2][3]. It appears in longevity and nootropic discussions as a neurotrophin mimic and is not approved for any use. Its connection to appearance is indirect and speculative: people interested in brain health and healthy ageing follow it as a candidate for protecting the nervous system, and this wiki does not describe any study of its effects on looks.
Studies so far come from a small number of related research reports on cell cultures and mouse models, including work with human stem cell-derived neurons [4].
infobox: Preclinical research only; not approved for any use

paras: BNN-20 is a synthetic analogue of DHEA, a steroid hormone. According to the authors who developed it, it is a small molecule that crosses the blood-brain barrier and has no endocrine side effects, which distinguishes it from natural neurotrophic factors such as BDNF that cannot readily cross the human barrier [1]. It is referred to in later papers as a synthetic, BDNF-mimicking microneurotrophin [2].

In weaver mice, long-term administration from postnatal day 1 to 21 almost fully protected dopaminergic neurons and their terminals. The authors attribute this to an anti-apoptotic effect probably mediated through TrkB receptor signalling via the PI3K-Akt-NF-kB pathway, an antioxidant effect, anti-inflammatory activity and restoration of BDNF levels [1].

A 2020 study reported that BNN-20 fully protected dopaminergic neurons even when administration began at a late stage, after more than 40 percent of neurons had degenerated. The anti-neuroinflammatory action was shown to be microglia-mediated at least in part: it partially reversed microglial hyperactivation and shifted polarisation toward the protective M2 phenotype, and BDNF levels that were severely reduced in the weaver midbrain returned to normal even after short-term administration [3].

A 2021 study in Stem Cell Research and Therapy assessed effects on neurogenesis in the substantia nigra of wild-type and weaver mice, building on the earlier neuroprotection data [2]. A 2022 paper in Cells used cultured postnatal brain neural stem cells to study divergence between neuronal and oligodendroglial fates and tested BNN-20 in those assays [5].

A 2024 paper extended the work in two ways: it tested BNN-20 on human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neural progenitors and neurons from healthy and parkinsonian donors, and on mouse progenitor grafts in late-stage weaver mice. BNN-20 had limited direct effects on the cultured human cells, marginally enhancing differentiation toward neurons and partly reversing the pathological phenotype of neurons from parkinsonian donors, had no effect on grafted mouse cells, but significantly enhanced an endogenous neurogenic response that the graft itself induced throughout the midbrain [4].
No studies found. Published research is limited to cell cultures and mouse models, including work on grafted neural progenitors [1][2][3][4].

The group's papers frame BNN-20 as a candidate for neuroprotective and pro-neurogenic therapy in Parkinson's disease, and the 2024 paper describes the human-cell and grafting experiments as extending the work in clinically relevant directions [4]. Whether the effects seen in the weaver mouse apply to people has not been tested.
